title: Legally Blonde 2: Red, White and Blonde
full_review:
Having already taken the "square" out of Harvard Square, America's favorite dizzy blonde sets her sights on giving Washington a makeover in the bubblegum comedy "Legally Blonde 2: Red, White & Blonde" (MGM).

Despite an effervescent performance by Reese Witherspoon, director Charles Herman-Wurmfeld's sequel to the 2001 sleeper hit lacks the freshness of its predecessor, rehashing many of the same blonde-fish-out-of-water jokes, making what were natural highlights in the original feel bottle-bought.

Taking up the action a few shopping sprees after the first film, Bel Air material girl and recent Harvard Law School graduate Elle Woods (Witherspoon) is juggling a demanding career as a rising young lawyer at one of Boston's top firms and planning the wedding of the century to her fiancee, Emmet (Luke Wilson). Yet upon discovering that the mother of her Chihuahua, Bruiser, won't be able to attend because she is being used as a test subject for cosmetics research, she decides to become the torchbearer for animal rights. Her zealous advocacy gets her fired when it turns out that the cosmetic company in question is one of the firm's most important clients.

In true never-underestimate-a-girl-with-a French-manicure-and-Harvard-law-degree frivolity, the well-coifed Elle packs her Prada bags and heads for the one town where vacuous thinking is de rigueur: Washington. She arrives in Jackie-O style, quickly painting the town pink. Her Cambridge connections land her a plum position on the staff of Hillaryesque Congresswoman Rudd (Sally Field). Of course, the icy reception extended by her fellow staff members, led by politically savvy Grace Rossiter (Regina King), lays the groundwork for the can't-judge-a-book-by-its-cover epiphanies down the pike.
With blithe flair and an impeccable fashion sense, Elle launches her crusade to make "Bruiser's Bill" the law of the land -- a feat easier said than done, especially for a towhead whose knowledge of Lincoln is limited to his poor choice of accessories, in one scene confiding to his statue "you were brave to wear that hat." She soon learns that there are forces working to derail her efforts and gets a crash-course in the Machiavellian machinations of corrupt backroom politics. Not one to be discouraged, Elle employs the aid of a sympathetic Deep Throat-like doorman (Bob Newhart) and a support network of her Delta Nu sorority sisters, turning the tables on her saboteurs and proving that you can't keep a good blonde down.

Of course, by time the final reel of the predictable fluff unspools, Elle not only gets the doggy legislation passed, but offers the joint houses of Congress a trite tutorial in democracy.

On more than one occasion the filmmaker genuflects at the altar of Frank Capra, paying heavy-handed homage to the heartfelt patriotism of "Mr. Smith Goes to Washington" -- even going so far as to include a clip of the 1939 Americana masterpiece starring Jimmy Stewart. As the idealistic Jefferson Smith, Stewart's impassioned filibustering leaves viewers itching to jump up and recite the Pledge of Allegiance, while Witherspoon's popcorn patriotism -- including such gag-worthy pabulum as "If we lose our voice, this country is in for a bad haircut" -- could inspire a petition to revoke her First Amendment right to free speech.
The golden-maned Witherspoon's smile lights up the screen, injecting an endearing buoyancy into what is otherwise Capitol Hill Barbie silliness. She inhabits her Jimmy Choo shoes with a sassy ebullience that should win her a "Farrah" from the blonde anti-defamation league. Regrettably, in this second tour of duty Witherspoon plays up Elle's Versace-vacuousness to the point of caricature, a marked digression from where the not-so-dumb blonde's character arc had led her at the end of the first film -- namely, valedictorian of Harvard Law School.

While many of the situations feel like retreads, the overall tone of "Legally Blonde 2" matches the cotton-candy flavor of the original, continuing its positive theme of believing in yourself and refraining from labels. However, one development that is more disturbing than white shoes after Labor Day is the not-so-subtle gay subplot involving Bruiser and a right-wing politico's Rottweiler, suspiciously sugarcoated so as to be easily digested by young audience members. This of course should come as no surprise given Herman-Wurmfeld's filmography, which includes the lesbian-themed "Kissing Jessica Stein" and a reference in the press notes to his "domestic partner."

Due to some mild sexual humor, a homosexual-themed subplot, as well as a smattering of crass language and an instance of profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
